newsitem.title: ALGERIA: Party of pro-president's men dominates Algeria poll.
newsitem.headline: Party of pro-president's men dominates Algeria poll.

text.p: Algeria's pro-presidential party, formed only two months ago, swept to victory on Friday in a general election which authorities hope will help end over five years of bloodshed they blame on Moslem fundamentalists.
Interior Minister Mustapha Benmansour told a news conference in the capital Algiers that the National Democratic Rally (RND) won 155 seats in the 380-seat parliament.
Second was the Islam-oriented Movement of a Peaceful Society (MPS) of Mahfoud Nahnah which took 69 seats, but which complained of "irregularities" in Thursday's ballot.

President Liamine Zeroual and his government see the vote as a basis for pulling the country out of the crisis into which it plunged in 1992. Violence erupted after the authorities in January that year cancelled a general election dominated by the now-banned Islamic Salvation Front (FIS).

About 60,000 people have died in the violence since then, and the authorities deployed more than 200,000 members of the security forces to guard polling stations across the oil and gas producing nation.

"This historic vote, which was not marred by any distortion, is an enormous progress and a great victory dedicated to the nation and future generations to build and strengthen democracy and the state of law," Benmansour told journalists.
With a final turnout of 65.49 percent, or nearly 11 million people across Africa's second largest country, the ballot gave the former sole ruling party, the National Liberation Front (FLN), 64 seats.

The FLN ruled for nearly three decades from independence from France in 1962 until youth riots in October 1988 forced the start of reform towards a multi-party system and away from a state-run economy.

The lowest turnout was in the capital Algiers -- under 44 percent -- which has been battered by much of the years of violence, including bombs last weekend which killed 22 people and wounded about 120.
Residents in the overcrowded city have been particularly hard hit by economic reforms, which brought praise overseas but caused hardship.
In one of only two reports of violence, MPS leader Nahnah said: "A real massacre took place in which there were (people) killed and wounded in Boudgham district."
He said the killing, in the western town of Tlemcen was "related to the elections", but refused to give any other detail. There was no official comment on the report or other confirmation.
The other report of violence also came from MPS sources who said earlier that two local poll observers had been wounded in a bomb blast in their car near the central town of Djelfa.

Sceptics in the capital doubt the level of violence will diminish soon because the new assembly lacks real power, which rests with the president, and it will not be able to push for dialogue with radical Islamists.

Another moderate Islamist party, Nahda, won 34 seats. Two rival secular parties, the Socialist Forces Front (FFS) of war veteran Hocine Ait Ahmed, and Rally for Culture and Democracy (RCD) of anti-Islamist hawk Said Saadi, each took 19.
Eleven independents were elected, with a handful of small parties taking one or two seats, and Louise Hanoune's Workers' Party, winning four.
RND spokesman Hamraoui Habib Chawki told Reuters before the results were announced that the proportional representation system of voting meant there would be no single dominant force in parliament.
"This will help the development of democracy and diversify the lower house," he said.
